items.content:
Emergency workers clear debris and damaged road infrastructure near a destroyed car after a Russian overnight strike in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP
Emergency workers clear debris and damaged road infrastructure near a destroyed car after a Russian overnight strike in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP
Ukraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky
Zelenskyy says ballistic missiles hit crowded areas with no military facilities nearby; truce comes amid reports of growing humanitarian crisis. What we know on day 1,707
Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded eight , with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying medical facilities and an intensive care unit had been damaged in the late Monday attack. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a ballistic missile attack had struck the grounds of a university campus in the Ukrainian capital. “The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media.
The strikes on Kyiv came hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was due to start , after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages . The truce, aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into Oleshky, was to begin at 3am local time (0100 GMT). No end date for the truce has been provided. The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces. Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US has said who would monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it. The Russian defence ministry said on Friday it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire. Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied.
Before the latest strikes on Kyiv, Zelenskyy highlighted ​Ukraine was still waiting for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on critical missile supplies . “We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the ⁠American side once again,” he said on X.
Romania said on Monday that a network “coordinated” from Russia was involved in starting a fire near an arms factory . The fire broke out on 14 September near an arms factory in the central city of Brasov and two Belarusians and a Ukrainian – residents in EU countries – were involved, authorities said. Two of them were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offences”, the office for organised crime said. The third is at large in Poland, it added. Russia’s embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations.
The attack in Brasov is the latest in a string of similar incidents in Europe , with Nato and the EU grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv. On Tuesday, Russia’s defence ⁠ministry said ⁠its ​forces ⁠had struck a ⁠vessel ​in ‌the Black ‌Sea that was transporting cargo ‌for the Ukrainian military, according to Russian ​media ​reports. Before Tuesday’s attack, at ​least eight cargo ​ships have been hit off the coast of Nato members Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing.
A Russian strike has damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv , Klitschko said on Tuesday, following reports of multiple ballistic missiles launched towards the Ukrainian capital. “A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged,” the city’s mayor wrote on Telegram. City officials said train services across the bridge had been suspended.
Ukraine’s military has begun using specialised aerial rescue drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield , carrying two stranded troops to safety near the Russian border in the first such operations. The newly developed StarGate drone, a six-rotor aircraft fitted with an enclosed evacuation capsule, was used in two separate missions over the past week, the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, an elite unit, said on Monday. Developed by Ukrainian technology company SkyFall, the drone is intended to reduce rescue times from hours to minutes, reaching hard-to-access combat zones currently served by unmanned ground vehicles.

If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, This Is the Vanguard ETF Warren Buffett Would Load Up On
The stock market has enjoyed a historical bull market over the last several years. Fueled primarily by artificial intelligence (AI), the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has climbed to all-time highs.
Naturally, some investors are questioning whether the rally can continue. If the stock market experiences a correction or even crashes in 2027, investors might be tempted to sell their stocks and wait for conditions to improve.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
I think doing the opposite could be considerably more rewarding in the long run. Legendary investor Warren Buffett has long supported a simple investment strategy that can help everyday investors build wealth through virtually any market environment. That strategy involves owning a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO).
Buffett earned a reputation for identifying undervalued businesses and holding on to them for decades. However, his advice for most investors is different from his own stock-picking approach . Rather than attempting to identify the next Nvidia , Buffett thinks most investors are better served by purchasing a diversified basket of America's largest companies.
In his 2013 shareholder letter, Buffett explained how he instructed the trustees managing his wife's inheritance to invest the funds. His recommendation was to allocate 10% to short-term government bonds and 90% to a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Buffett specified his preferred provider, writing, "I suggest Vanguard's."
Interestingly, Berkshire Hathaway previously owned shares of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. According to 13F filings, Berkshire held 43,000 shares of the fund before liquidating the position during the fourth quarter of 2024.
Image source: Getty Images. Why the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is a great long-term option
The beauty of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF lies in its composition. Its holdings span technology, healthcare, financial services, consumer products, industrial businesses, and other industries. This diversification is important because each sector performs differently under certain economic conditions.
The S&P 500 has demonstrated resilience throughout history. During the dot-com crash, the index declined 49% between 2000 and 2002. During the 2008 financial crisis, it lost roughly 57% from its 2007 peak to its 2009 bottom. More recently, the S&P 500 endured a bear market in 2022 as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to combat inflation.
The chart depicts recessions in the grey columns. Despite a number of setbacks, the S&P 500 consistently bounced back and reached new highs. This resilience reflects a distinct characteristic of the index: Its composition changes over time. Companies that become irrelevant are eventually replaced by stronger businesses, allowing the index to evolve alongside the American economy.
VOO also offers the advantage of low costs. The fund charges an annual expense ratio of just 0.03%. This means you pay $3 a year for every $10,000 invested. Keeping expenses low allows investors to retain more of their gains, which can make a meaningful difference as your contributions compound over decades.
A stock market crash could create a generational buying opportunity
One of the biggest mistakes investors make during market downturns is assuming that cratering stock prices automatically signal poor investment opportunities. In reality, market crashes allow patient investors to buy the dip in quality businesses at substantially lower prices.
Of course, no one knows exactly when a market crash will occur or how long a recovery will take. This is why investors shouldn't wait for a crash before buying a stake in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. A more prudent strategy is to use dollar-cost averaging, investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of market conditions.
Investors with long time horizons and financial flexibility will come to find that market downturns offer lucrative wealth-creation opportunities rather than reasons to run for the hills. Ultimately, Buffett's investment philosophy is rooted in a simple practice: Owning a diversified basket of blue chip American businesses over long periods is often more rewarding than attempting to predict every market fluctuation. If the stock market crashes in 2027, I see the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF as one of the smartest investments to accumulate for the next decade and beyond.

items.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
items.summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
items.content:
Image caption, The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or water
By Paul Kirby ,Â  Europe digital editor ,Â  Olga Malchevska Â  and Â  Dan Johnson ,Â  in Kyiv
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.
That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".
A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
Image caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.
Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Image caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.
Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.
Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

items.content:
Share Iran’s calculations as US escalation looms: Trust, midterms, Hormuz on social media
A woman walks past a mural in Tehran [File: Atta Kenare/AFP]
As regional powers step up diplomatic efforts to prevent another escalation in the eight-month United States-Israel war on Iran, Tehran is showing little sign of backing down from its red lines.
The announcement by China on Tuesday that Beijing will be sending an envoy to relevant countries in the region soon to help avoid another round of escalation highlights the growing urgency of finding a peaceful solution to a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and spilled over across the region.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Iran’s authorities take ‘self-sacrifice’ mobilisation campaign nationwide
list 2 of 3 US military says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil
list 3 of 3 Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan agree to continue talks for peace
On Monday, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye – the three nations which signed the Mecca defence pact in August – met with high-ranking Iranian officials, promising to continue discussions related to “peace and security” in the region.
However, Tehran appears determined not to budge on its demands, particularly as it holds considerable leverage over the future of maritime trade in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) were shipped before the war.
“Iran’s priority is not simply to secure another ceasefire, but to end the war permanently and establish deterrence so that the cycle of military attacks by the US and Israel does not keep repeating itself,” Negar Mortazavi, editor and host of The Iran Podcast, told Al Jazeera.
Tehran continues to insist on sanctions relief, an end to the US naval blockade on its ports in the Gulf and guarantees that the US will not renew attacks, in exchange for helping to resume normal traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. The US wants Iran to give up more before a final peace settlement is negotiated – including making concessions about its nuclear programme.
Experts say Iran’s current calculations are being driven by several factors, including its deep distrust of Washington – which has launched strikes on Iran three times since June 2025 while conducting talks – the belief that continued economic pressure could force more attractive US concessions, and much-anticipated elections in Israel and the US this week and next.
At the heart of Iran’s position is a belief that previous diplomatic efforts have failed to provide sufficient protection against renewed US and Israeli attacks. The US and Israel launched the first strikes of the war on February 28, just as peace talks were ongoing in Oman. Last year, Israel launched its 12-day war on Iran in June, which the US joined.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker a memorandum of understanding in June this year aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, ending the US blockade of Iranian ports and laying down the conditions for the start of negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme.
But the arrangement quickly unravelled as both sides resumed attacks, leading to sustained US attacks on Iran for several weeks in July, followed by retaliatory strikes from Iran on US military assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf countries, as well as in Jordan.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy (CIP), said the failure of that arrangement had hardened Tehran’s position.
“Iran believes previous negotiations and ceasefire arrangements failed to protect it from renewed military attacks, and it is therefore seeking more tangible and durable guarantees,” he told Al Jazeera.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has remained ambiguous over what course of action he will take in the near future. “My question is, do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off?” Trump told reporters on Sunday. He had previously said attacks on Iran would not take place until after the US midterms on November 3.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said last week that the country’s armed forces were prepared to respond to any new attacks , including by invading Tehran’s neighbours and hitting bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy in its war with the US.
He also said Iran would only reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin peace talks once Washington took concrete steps to rebuild trust, including meeting Iran’s latest set of conditions – suspending sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and giving concrete assurances that it will not begin strikes again.
The US midterms next week, when all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats will be up for grabs, will determine which party has control of the US Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. The war, already deeply unpopular with Americans, is becoming an increasingly contentious domestic issue.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey earlier this month found just 34 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of the conflict – his lowest rating during either of his presidential terms. Republican majorities in both houses of Congress are already wafer-thin – at 53-47 (including two independents who vote with Democrats) in the Senate and 218-214 in the House.
The war has also driven up energy prices – particularly diesel, which has nearly doubled in price, causing a major burden for farmers and small businesses – adding to concerns about inflation and affordability that are dominating the election campaign.
Some reports citing Iranian officials say Tehran may be deliberately prolonging negotiations to deny Trump any sort of political victory before the elections.
A Republican setback could further constrain Trump’s room for manoeuvre, particularly if Democrats gain congressional control and increase scrutiny of the administration’s conduct of the war.
“Tehran wants to teach a lesson to Washington, including future American presidents, that attacking Iran comes with a high price,” analyst Mortazavi said.
“Its deterrence strategy is multilayered, aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs that extend well beyond the battlefield.”
Before the US midterms is Israel’s election on Tuesday, which introduces another dimension to Iran’s calculations. A defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could complicate renewing joint attacks with the US on Iran, as experts say he was the main force behind Trump greenlighting the war.
While some believe an opposition victory led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot could potentially ease regional tensions, Netanyahu’s removal would not necessarily translate into a softer Israeli position towards Iran.
Eisenkot is himself a former military chief, and has repeatedly expressed concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme and regional influence.
Nevertheless, Mortazavi said, while Iranian officials are closely watching the political consequences of the war for both Washington and Israel, they recognise the danger of renewed escalation after the elections, “making a durable diplomatic settlement even more urgent”.
Iran’s control over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains one of its strongest bargaining chips.
The waterway carried about one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the war began on February 28, giving Tehran considerable leverage over global oil markets.
October has recorded the highest number of attacks on commercial shipping around Hormuz, according to data collected by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Brent crude surged above $117 a barrel last week – compared with about $72 pre-war – following Iranian attacks on tankers, while shipping through the strait remains nowhere near pre-war levels.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, said he believes Iran is deliberately exploiting this economic pressure as part of a wider contest of endurance with Washington.
“They know they are in an attritional race with the US to see who breaks first,” Beauchamp told Al Jazeera. “For now, however, they are happy to keep attacking shipping to push prices higher.”
The latest diplomatic initiative reflects a growing concern among regional powers about the consequences of another round of fighting.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye agreed with Iranian officials on Monday to continue discussions about regional peace and security, amid fears that the conflict could escalate again.
The talks in Tehran come amid heightened regional tensions following weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, who are also engaged in a conflict with forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government.
Pakistan and Turkiye maintain close strategic ties with Saudi Arabia and have committed to supporting Riyadh militarily under the recently established Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between the three Muslim-majority nations.
Political analyst Rami Khouri, a nonresident fellow at the Arab Center in Washington DC, said the meeting had several objectives, some more immediate than others.
“The most immediate goal: to de-escalate and to try to return to the diplomatic process, to have a permanent ceasefire, and then define the issues and address them with much stronger mediation, supported by these three countries [Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye] and maybe others,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He added that talks could mark the beginning of a shift away from a regional security order dominated by Washington, towards one in which Middle East countries and other regional nations can exercise greater influence.
Meanwhile, CIP’s Toossi said regional powers are increasingly recognising that their own security cannot be separated from that of Iran, despite their differences with Tehran.
“It will be difficult to stabilise Yemen while the wider US-Iran confrontation continues, just as it will be difficult to reach a durable settlement with Iran while regional military escalation remains a constant threat,” he said.
Ultimately, however, the biggest obstacle remains Iran’s lack of trust in Washington, Iran Podcast host Mortazavi said.
“After two wars, Tehran is deeply sceptical of American commitments and wants concrete guarantees that any agreement will not simply become another temporary pause before the next attack,” she said.
“Iran is willing to negotiate and has already demonstrated flexibility by presenting a proposal to end the war. But Tehran believes it retains significant leverage, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, and will not surrender that leverage under military or economic pressure. items.content:
Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long discusses the Federal Reserve's upcoming interest rate decisions.
The Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest interest rate decision on Wednesday with the midterm elections less than a week away.
Policymakers at the Fed say they avoid letting politics influence their monetary policy moves, and can be hesitant to hike or cut interest rates at meetings that occur ahead of the election.
Inflation has remained stubbornly high and the September consumer price index (CPI) data showed inflation rose faster than expected, with headline CPI rising 0.6% on a monthly basis and 3.7% from a year ago. The latter figure is well above the central bank's 2% inflation target.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told FOX Business in an interview that while the September inflation data was hotter than expected and raised the prospects of an October rate hike, the Fed is likely to wait to "hike again in December."
CONSUMER INFLATION ROSE FASTER THAN EXPECTED IN SEPTEMBER, CPI REPORT SHOWS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and policymakers are expected to hold rates steady this week. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"This hotter than expected inflation data did increase the chance of an October rate hike , but it's a very high bar to increase in October, they would do it within a week of the election. I know they like to say that they're not political, but it's a high bar for October," she explained.
"Right now, this data indicates that the Fed needs to act again, but it's not a five-alarm fire. They don't have to act immediately, they could wait until December."
"The reality is, gas prices have come down a little bit since the September highs, so we would expect the October data – you know, it won't be great, but it could be a little bit cooler than what we're seeing today. And the Fed has a reasonable case to say, we're probably still gonna hike, but let's wait a few more weeks and see just how broad-based this problem really is," Long said.
FEDERAL RESERVE HIKES INTEREST RATES FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2023 AMID STUBBORN INFLATION
The market expects the Fed to hold rates steady this week, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 90.6% probability of rates remaining at their current target range of 3.75% to 4% – up from 84.5% a week ago and 35.8% last month.
For the Fed's meeting in mid-December, the tool shows a 75.1% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike, which could mark the resumption of the rate-hiking cycle if inflation remains elevated.
WHY THE FED ISN'T READY TO DECLARE VICTORY ON INFLATION
Inflation rose faster than expected in September and remains well above the central bank's 2% target. (Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images)
"The Federal Reserve will definitely hike interest rates again, probably in December," Long said. "The big question is how many more times do they have to hike after that? And what was scary in this latest inflation data for September is to see so many areas of hot inflation: to see used car prices, airfares, recreation costs, auto repair costs, buying a used car, medical costs."
"The story really is starting to take shape that it's probably going to take a couple more hikes in 2027, and this higher-for-longer borrowing costs and mortgage rates well above 7% is going to stick around for at least a year, maybe longer," Long said.
The CME FedWatch tool shows the market is anticipating multiple rate hikes by March, with a 46.5% chance that rates will be 50 basis points higher than they are now at a range of 4.25% to 4.5%.

items.title: I Saw Ukraine’s Rapid Adaptation Cycle in Action, and This is What the US Military Should Learn from It - Modern War Institute -
items.summary: I Saw Ukraine’s Rapid Adaptation Cycle in Action, and This is What the US Military Should Learn from It  Modern War Institu
items.content:
I Saw Ukraine’s Rapid Adaptation Cycle in Action, and This is What the US Military Should Learn from It
During my time in Ukraine I saw more than a country at war. I saw a defense innovation ecosystem in which the daily imperative to survive drove rapid learning and adaptation. It also exposed a serious weakness in the American model of military technology development. A Ukrainian drone can be jammed, modified to counter the jamming, and sent back into the fight in less time than it takes the US defense system to process a request. That gap is more than a bureaucratic frustration. It is a strategic vulnerability.
When Russian forces jammed a drone’s signal, Ukrainian engineers often developed a fix within days, and sometimes within hours. They changed frequencies, replaced antennas, or adopted new navigation methods. Once the solution worked, it got back to the front quickly. In many cases the drone was flying again within a day or two. As I watched this responsiveness in action, I kept comparing it to how the same problem would move through our system. A US unit that identifies an urgent requirement for change submits a request. The issue enters a process built for review and control. If it is serious enough it may be classified as a Joint Urgent Operational Need or a Joint Emergent Operational Need. Even on that accelerated track it can take up to a year to field an initial solution and as long as two years to deploy it fully. By then the threat may have changed several times. The system will have done what it was designed to do, but too slowly to matter.
The problem is that we do not evaluate our defense industry, or our own institutions, based on how well they adapt when conditions change. We evaluate them based on how well they perform against requirements written in advance. The central flaw is not a lack of talent or technology. It is that we reward compliance over adaptation. We write a requirement, give it to industry, and then judge the final product against that same requirement. In effect we provide the answer key and then reward companies for following it. That approach may work for predictable procurement. It does not work for war.
Even our existing rapid acquisition pathways, including the Middle Tier of Acquisition and urgent operational needs processes, still largely judge solutions against requirements written in advance. They can accelerate delivery of a planned solution, but they do not systematically measure or reward a company’s ability to adapt when the threat changes after the requirement is locked. War is dynamic. Adversaries do not announce their next moves, and the most dangerous threats are often the ones that did not exist when the requirement was drafted. The jamming frequencies used against US systems in a future conflict will not match the ones described in a document written years earlier. They will be the ones an adversary developed last week. Yet we continue to favor companies skilled at preparing for planned events rather than those capable of solving new problems quickly. These skill sets are fundamentally different. One produces compliance. The other fosters adaptation. Innovation experts describe this as the adaptability gap , the distance between how much an organization claims to value adaptability and how much it actually invests in it. In the US defense sector this gap has become structural.
If the threat changes in real time, the Department of Defense’s evaluation model must change with it. Rather than judging fixed products against static standards alone, the department should assess a company’s broader innovation ecosystem and its ability to adapt capability at operational speed. To implement this change, the department should update DFARS 215.304 . That provision already governs evaluation factors used in departmental source selections and provides precedents for assessing attributes beyond the immediate end item, including small business participation, manufacturing readiness, supply chain risk, sustainment, and supplier risk. The regulation therefore already recognizes that a company’s ability to deliver capability depends on more than whether a product meets a point-in-time specification. The central question should be whether its engineers, software teams, production lines, legal staff, and product designers can absorb new battlefield data and convert it into a workable solution in weeks rather than years.
That shift requires new criteria. Contracts could specify maximum two-week turnaround for software updates. This timeline is fast enough to drive real change from today’s multimonth cycles, yet realistic enough to assess responsiveness. Procurement processes could include demonstration phases in which companies must design, test, and field modifications within defined periods using recent threat scenarios. The goal is not to weaken standards. It is to operationalize them in alignment with the demands of modern conflict.
The Department of Defense already has both an immediate mechanism to implement this change and an enduring organization to scale it. Under Project Agincourt, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) is directed to lead the near-term transition and develop the pathway to the Autonomous Warfare Command . While carrying out its current responsibilities, the DRPM-UxS can pilot a revised acquisition model for testing adaptability.
Consider how we often test autonomous systems today. Requirements may state that platforms must operate in a contested electronic warfare environment. Manufacturers arrive at the test range already knowing the frequencies they will face. They prepare for those expected conditions, pass the test, and move toward procurement. A more realistic evaluation would expose the system to the latest electronic warfare signals captured from active battlefields, signals that may not have existed when the requirements were drafted. The system will likely fail. That is not the end of the test. It is the beginning of the real one. At that point we should measure how quickly a company can diagnose the problem, rewrite the software, validate the fix, and scale it into production. If that timeline is measured in years rather than weeks, the company should not win the contract.
Some will argue that the United States is not at war and therefore lacks access to the right battlefield data. That is not a sufficient excuse. Ukrainian partners confront these threats every day. They offer two clear ways to make our testing more realistic. The first is data. Ukrainian partners can share current threat information, from captured jamming signals to evolving enemy tactics, that can keep US testing relevant. The second is access to the environment itself. Ukraine’s Brave1 defense technology cluster runs a program called Test in Ukraine that allows systems to be exposed to live Russian threats in operational conditions. That model is already expanding. New initiatives linking Ukrainian defense firms with NATO partners are creating pathways for allied companies to test systems against real-world threats and learn from one of the most combat-tested innovation ecosystems in the world. The infrastructure for more realistic testing is not hypothetical. It is already taking shape.
This approach comes with legal, security, and intelligence-sharing challenges. Sensitive battlefield data cannot simply move across borders without safeguards. While such concerns are valid, they are implementation problems, not reasons for inaction. With the right protocols and close coordination, realistic testing is possible.
This approach will fail, however, if the Department of Defense demands adaptability from industry while exempting itself from the same standard. The department is emphasizing adaptation, but meanwhile, regulations and policy lag. Today’s incentive structures do not reward program managers for learning quickly. They reward them for clean audits, predictable timelines, and avoiding budget turbulence.
During my time in Special Forces acquisition we had a simple motto: Fail fast. Learn quickly whether something works, stop funding what does not, and move resources to what does. Scaling that mindset across the broader defense enterprise will not be easy, but it is necessary. Performance metrics should track how quickly teams respond to emerging threats and how effectively they adapt. Pilot programs should reward timely iteration, even when it includes short-term failure. Promotions and recognition should go to leaders who move quickly and extract useful lessons from rapid testing, not just those who hit traditional milestones. If we are serious about closing the adaptability gap, we must be willing to accept the risk and invest the necessary money, time, and people.
Testing for adaptability does involve risk. Some tests will fail. Some funding will go to efforts that do not succeed. That is not waste. It is the cost of learning faster than the adversary. A culture that treats every failed test as a scandal will produce a military that looks efficient on paper and loses in practice.
Ukraine did not build an adaptive defense industrial base because it had perfectly written requirements. It built one because it had no alternative. The old model would have cost it the war, so Ukraine replaced it with an ecosystem that learns under pressure. The United States still has time to reform how it tests, fields, and rewards innovation. But that window is narrowing. Russia is adapting in real time, and China is building the industrial and mobilization capacity to outproduce and outlast its opponents in a high-intensity fight—a scale the United States is not yet built to match. The central question is no longer whether America can build advanced systems, but whether those systems and the institutions behind them can evolve fast enough to matter.
Colonel Rachael Hoagland is an Army acquisition corps officer with more than twenty-nine years of service. She most recently served in a dual-hatted role as Science and Technology Division chief and director of the Joint Capabilities Acquisition Cell, and she spent nine months in Ukraine working directly with operational units, the Ministry of Defence, the Defence Procurement Agency, and the domestic defense industry.
The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

Nvidia (NVDA) shares rose 1.5% after the world's most valuable public company said it will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering.
Memory and other AI-tied stocks rose further after beginning the week with gains. Sherwin-Williams (SHW) fell 1.5%, Whirlpool (WHR) declined 1%, and Corning (GLW) and Coca-Cola (KO) ticked lower. Visa (V) was 1% lower ahead of its results after markets close today.

U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude futures pulled back 1.7% to $100 a barrel in recent trading. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, declined 1.7% to below $114.
The 10-year Treasury yield was up less than one basis point to near 5.00%. Bitcoin was trading around $80,400, up slightly over the past 24 hours. The U.S. dollar index , which tracks the value of the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, was 0.3% higher at 102.25. Gold futures rose 0.9% to $4,075 an ounce.

Economists expect the Fed to raise rates at future meetings to combat high inflation, but say there is no rush to raise them for a second consecutive meeting following September's rate hike. Financial markets are pricing in just an 11% likelihood the Fed will raise rates this week, per CME FedWatch.

items.title: West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on
items.summary: Millions face acute hunger in Sudan as conflict, drought and funding cuts aggravate the humanitarian crisis.
items.content:
Image caption, War in Sudan has led to the worst humanitarian crisis with more than 33 million people in need of assistance according to the WHO
The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine.
In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production.
"There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted.
The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people.
The statement , external was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website.
It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger.
"I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.
While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September.
"Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added.
The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action.
The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El NiÃ±o, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan.
"The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access.
In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.
The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

items.content:
China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs
Beijing’s evolving industrial playbook is taking shape in Morocco.
By Aaron Glasserman , a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, and Jessie Jiexi Lin , a student pursuing a master’s in public administration at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.
Workers in dark uniforms and blue baseball caps inspect the metal frames of silver, unpainted electric vehicles along a brightly lit assembly line on a factory floor. The line of cars extends backward to the far wall, with similar small groups of workers bustling around each one.
Workers check vehicle frames on the production line for electric vehicle maker Zeekr at its factory in Ningbo, China, on May 29, 2025. Kevin Frayer/Getty Images
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
The more consequential story—that will likely make Chinese EVs even more competitive in the near future—is Beijing’s evolving approach to overseas industrial policy. At the core of this approach is an increasingly coordinated model of public- and private-sector activity.
State-owned enterprises (SOE) lay the groundwork for favorable investment environments abroad by undertaking massive infrastructure projects and securing access to strategic resources. Boosted by Beijing’s diplomatic ties and international clout, private companies leverage these state-backed platforms as a springboard for trade by bringing in investment, production capacity, and industry-specific expertise.
The advantages of this approach for Beijing—and the challenge that it poses to foreign companies—are already on full display in Morocco, where years of existing strategic investment, infrastructure development, and geopolitical maneuvering are pushing China closer to vertically integrating EV supply chains, bypassing tariffs, and further reshaping Europe’s auto industry.
It is only in recent years that Morocco has emerged as a key node in China’s EV empire.
For decades, Beijing maintained much closer ties with Morocco’s neighbor and rival, Algeria, but that began to change in the early 2010s as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) took off. In 2016, Morocco joined the growing ranks of countries signing “strategic partnerships” with China, making mutual commitments to expand economic cooperation and recognize each other’s core interests.
The next year, Morocco officially entered the BRI, and China has since poured millions of dollars into Morocco’s energy and transportation sectors . Almost a decade later, that economic relationship has expanded dramatically: In March, China’s committed investment in the country exceeded $10 billion , concentrated mostly in the EV and energy sectors.
China’s EV manufacturing capacity in Morocco builds on years of large-scale, state-backed investment in transportation infrastructure and natural resources. Over the past decade, Chinese SOEs have collaborated on major infrastructure and development projects in Morocco, including bridges , highways , and smart cities . Some of these are directly relevant to the EV industry, such as the chemical processing unit in Khouribga, home to one of the world’s biggest reserves of phosphate, which is critical for EV battery production .
This SOE-led scramble for resources and construction-heavy projects paved the way for private Chinese companies in the EV sector to establish footholds in Morocco and ship to overseas markets. Tanger Tech City, China’s SOE-led flagship collaboration with Morocco, is located less than 30 miles from Tanger Med, the largest container port in Africa. Taking advantage of no-fee business registration and tax-free dividends, private Chinese companies—including the global battery giant BTR New Material Group as well as tire manufacturers Sentury Tire and Guizhou Tyre—have established or announced plans to establish production bases in the industrial zone.
Elsewhere in the country, major private investments include battery manufacturer Gotion’s $1.3 billion factory and a $2 billion joint-venture battery materials factory between China’s CNGR Advanced Material and the Moroccan private equity firm Al Mada.
This isn’t to deny the role of subsidies and preferential financing, which Beijing sees as key tools for supporting companies that are expanding internationally. A 2024 directive , for instance, called on Chinese financial institutions to improve credit approval and lending procedures and to enhance cross-border settlement to “better support companies expanding into international markets.” Closer collaboration among Chinese banks, semi-official trade organizations, and Moroccan banks has also helped to streamline financing and channel investment into the African market.
But these policies are useful to Chinese firms because they are operating in an industrial landscape that SOEs have already shaped, with relatively easy access to necessary resources and infrastructure.
China’s success with this approach has only been possible because it also advances Rabat’s desire to expand domestic manufacturing capability and position Morocco as Africa’s next industrial powerhouse. Chinese investment is expected to generate sorely needed jobs; Morocco’s unemployment rate has hardly dipped below 10 percent for the past decade, and youth unemployment in cities stands at a staggering 47 percent. Officials claim that the Gotion factory alone will create 17,000 local jobs, including 2,300 high-skilled positions.
Beijing has coupled this economic engagement with a subtle diplomatic shift in favor of Rabat’s claims over Western Sahara . For decades, China has avoided explicitly backing either Morocco or Western Sahara, though its rhetoric often leaned toward the latter—and thus to the latter’s main sponsor, Algiers . With one exception in 2018, it consistently voted in favor of United Nations Security Council resolutions extending the peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara and affirming support for the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination.
However, in recent years, China has done an about-face. In 2024, its Ministry of Foreign Affairs implicitly acknowledged the importance of the Western Sahara question for Rabat, stating , “China supports Morocco in maintaining national security and stability and is ready to work with Morocco to continue firmly supporting each other on issues concerning their respective core interests.” Then, last fall, Beijing abstained on the most recent U.N. resolution on the matter, which for the first time endorsed Rabat’s proposal to formally establish Western Sahara as an autonomous region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The full payoff of China’s Moroccan gambit will materialize if and when localized EV manufacturing matures, which could take years. That is still a tall order, as evidenced by the recent shelving of a BYD assembly plant project that had been stalled since 2017 due to budget issues and limited local charging infrastructure, according to a company executive.
Though Chinese automakers are not yet building assembly plants in Morocco, the country matters for everything “upstream” of assembly. It is becoming an integrated ecosystem for the production of batteries, tires, and other components, which reduces Chinese EV companies’ reliance on direct shipments from China and lowers costs for Chinese assembly plants in Europe and Africa.
Morocco also offers Chinese firms convenient access to the European market through the Tanger Med port and—more importantly—a rules-based pathway through Brussels’s tightening trade defenses . Currently, the EU imposes duties of up to 35 percent on EVs manufactured in China. However, vehicles that qualify as Moroccan in origin can enter the European market duty-free. That includes vehicles assembled in Morocco, so long as foreign parts make up less than 45 percent of the finished vehicle’s ex-works price.
In short, if Chinese EV companies succeed in establishing vehicle assembly factories and fully integrating supply chains in Morocco, they will be able to sell vehicles to Europe under a “Made in Morocco” label, avoiding both the 10 percent EU standard automobile tariff and the additional punitive tariff on Chinese-made EVs—reducing the total tariff effect from as much as 45 percent to zero. This would pose an unprecedented threat to what remains one of the EU’s most important industries .
China is rolling out this coordinated approach to overseas industrial policy elsewhere to varying degrees.
In Thailand, for example, China is a key investor in the Eastern Economic Corridor, a flagship regional development initiative anchored by a high-speed railway that will connect several Thai cities and seaports to China. The corridor has, in turn, provided an attractive environment for private Chinese investment. China is now the corridor’s largest source of foreign direct investment, primarily in the EV sector and related industries. Like Tanger Tech City, the corridor offers private Chinese companies major tax incentives and more convenient access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ market.
The United Arab Emirates offers another example. In 2017, Chinese SOE Jiangsu Provincial Overseas Cooperation and Investment Company Limited (JOCIC) partnered with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop an industrial and special economic zone inside the Khalifa Port’s free trade zone. JOCIC set up a wholly owned UAE subsidiary to manage the park, which lets it attract Chinese private capital while insulating the parent company from project-level and geopolitical risk. The park’s location provides Chinese companies with a convenient base for expansion into the Persian Gulf and wider Middle Eastern markets, along with exemptions from value-added tax and other financial incentives . As of 2025, more than 40 Chinese companies had collectively committed more than $700 million to the park, with a focus on EVs and renewable energy.
Beijing has long seen its SOEs as tools for advancing its broader economic interests. As China in recent years has emphasized “small and beautiful” projects , the SOE-led megaprojects are often viewed as commercially disappointing holdovers from an earlier and more profligate era of BRI. Nevertheless, under this coordinated strategy, Beijing has been able to capitalize on the advantages secured by past infrastructure projects and deepen its presence in the overseas market.
As governments in industrialized economies respond to China’s surge of high-value manufactured exports, they must recognize how the sources of Chinese firms’ advantages are changing. Today, those advantages come not just from subsidies and cheap credit at home but also from integrated ecosystems abroad, built through coordination between public and private enterprise.
This means that Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs and the recently announced limits on hybrid EVs imported from China, on their own, are unlikely to stem the tide of EVs made by Chinese firms operating around the world. China’s rivals—even in industrialized economies—will struggle to compete unless they can coordinate across borders and build supply chains and infrastructure that leverage or, far less plausibly, completely sidestep what China has already put in place.

U.S. Stock Futures Point Higher as AI Developments and Earnings Support Market Recovery: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Nasdaq sign on building ©ajay_suresh U.S. stock futures indicated a higher opening on Tuesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend Monday's gains as investors assessed developments in artificial intelligence, quarterly corporate earnings and the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Renewed attention to AI-related companies followed Anthropic's public filing for an initial public offering and an expanded partnership between Nvidia and Meta Platforms.
Corporate earnings also influenced premarket trading, with JetBlue Airways and Corning advancing, while Whirlpool declined following disappointing quarterly results and a reduction in its annual revenue guidance.
Investors were also preparing for Wednesday's Federal Reserve policy announcement, with interest rates widely expected to remain unchanged.
Artificial Intelligence Developments Support U.S. Equity Futures
AI-related developments remained a focus for investors following recent volatility in technology shares.
Anthropic's public filing for an initial public offering contributed to renewed interest in the sector, following concerns about the financing requirements associated with large-scale AI infrastructure investment.
Those concerns had weighed on U.S. equities late in the previous week, particularly as investors assessed the implications of debt-financed spending on computing capacity and related infrastructure.
Attention also turned to an expanded collaboration between Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META).
The companies announced plans to broaden their work on Muse and the Muse family of artificial intelligence models.
As part of the arrangement, Nvidia said it would invest $3 billion in Meta, which is pursuing plans to raise up to $95 billion through equity financing.
The announcements provided additional developments for investors assessing spending and commercial activity across the AI industry.
JetBlue and Corning Advance Following Quarterly Earnings
Several companies recorded notable premarket movements following their latest financial announcements.
JetBlue Airways (NASDAQ:JBLU) shares climbed 13.9% before the opening bell, despite the airline reporting a third-quarter loss larger than analysts had anticipated.
The company also indicated that it expects further operating margin expansion during the fourth quarter.
Corning (NYSE:GLW) shares advanced in premarket trading after the glass manufacturer reported third-quarter revenue and earnings above Wall Street estimates.
The results contributed to company-specific share price movements ahead of the regular trading session.
Whirlpool Declines After Lowering Annual Revenue Guidance
Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR) shares fell 7.2% in premarket trading after the appliance manufacturer reported third-quarter financial results below analyst expectations.
The company also reduced its full-year revenue guidance.
The announcement added to investor attention on corporate profitability and demand conditions across consumer-related industries.
Whirlpool's decline contrasted with the premarket advances recorded by JetBlue and Corning, reflecting different responses to the latest earnings announcements.
The Federal Reserve's upcoming monetary policy announcement remained a central consideration for financial markets.
The central bank is scheduled to announce its interest rate decision on Wednesday, with market participants widely expecting policymakers to maintain current borrowing costs.
Investors will also examine the accompanying policy statement for indications of how officials assess inflation, economic activity and the future direction of interest rates.
The pending decision could contribute to restrained trading activity ahead of the announcement.
Wall Street Rebounds Following Previous Week's Declines
U.S. equities recovered on Monday after recording losses during the final two sessions of the previous week.
The Nasdaq Composite advanced 214.04 points, or 0.8%, to close at 26,169.38.
The S&P 500 gained 53.09 points, or 0.7%, finishing at 7,676.77, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average increased 146.32 points, or 0.3%, to 52,361.58.
Although all three indices ended the session higher, they closed below their intraday peaks.
The recovery followed a period of selling pressure that had pushed the Nasdaq to its lowest closing level since early August and the S&P 500 to a one-month closing low.
Buying activity on Monday included purchases of shares that had declined during the preceding sessions.
Lower Oil Prices and Middle East Diplomacy Influence Trading
Energy prices also contributed to the market backdrop, with U.S. crude oil futures declining 1.5%.
The decrease followed reports that Saudi Arabia's defense minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, had travelled to Tehran for discussions with senior Iranian officials.
The meetings were intended to address efforts to reduce tensions associated with the conflict in the Middle East.
The decline in crude oil prices coincided with the recovery in U.S. equities, as investors monitored geopolitical developments and their implications for energy markets.
Semiconductor and Networking Stocks Lead Monday's Gains
Technology-related sectors recorded some of the largest advances during Monday's trading session.
The NYSE Arca Networking Index rose 2.9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 2.8%.
Computer hardware and software companies also recorded increases, alongside oil services stocks.
Brokerage shares moved lower, contrasting with gains across several technology-related industries.
The sector movements reflected renewed buying interest in parts of the technology market following the declines recorded late in the previous week.
Investors Await Fed Announcement as Earnings Season Continues
Tuesday's expected higher opening follows a recovery in U.S. equities supported by AI-related developments, selected corporate earnings announcements and lower crude oil prices.
The Nasdaq, S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average all advanced on Monday, with semiconductor and networking stocks recording notable gains.
Premarket trading indicated further company-specific movements, including increases in JetBlue and Corning shares and a decline in Whirlpool.
Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve's Wednesday policy announcement, alongside additional corporate earnings and developments in AI investment.

Talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday have raised hopes of a de-escalation in the regional conflict.
U.S. President Donald Trump is weighing whether to pursue an agreement with Tehran or launch further military action.
Markets beginning to catch onto 'revenge of the old economy' trade, says expert
Crude oil prices fell for the second consecutive session Tuesday, driven by a renewed diplomatic push to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 1.7% to close at $113.88 a barrel. U.S.  West Texas Intermediate futures fell 1.8% to settle at $99.90 a barrel.
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met with his top national security official Mohsen Rezaei to discuss the Islamic Republic's conditions for ending the war with the U.S., according to a Tuesday post in English to the supreme leader's social media account .
Khamenei said the current state of "neither war nor peace" needs to end, according to the post. He discussed "safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control" over the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's defense minister and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian held direct talks in Tehran on Monday to de-escalate tensions. Senior military and intelligence officials from Pakistan and Turkey, who are allied with the Saudis, also participated.
Saudi Arabia has come under repeated attack from Iran-allied Houthi militants in recent weeks. The Houthis have bombed energy infrastructure as well as civilian targets such as airports.
The Houthi strikes threaten to disrupt Saudi oil exports, which have proven resilient during eight months of conflict in the region.
Iran Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said the talks in Tehran were a step toward regional security cooperation and further consultations are possible, according to the state media outlet Tasnim .
The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.
Brent oil prices are expected to remain near $110 a barrel through the end of the year, said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo in a Tuesday note. The oil market hasn't normalized yet even though exports from the Middle East have increased compared to prior stages of the war, Staunovo said.
"Vessels remain exposed to attacks, insurance and freight costs have risen sharply, and increased ship-to-ship transfers required to cross the Strait of Hormuz are absorbing tanker capacity," the analyst said.
Global oil inventories have fallen by around 500 million barrels since February, Staunovo said. The release of strategic stockpiles by governments is largely over, he said. Commercial inventories will fall more sharply in the coming months as a consequence if security conditions don't improve, the analyst said.
"With global visible oil inventories at multi-year lows and likely to take time to rebuild once the conflict is resolved, oil prices may also remain higher for longer as inventories first need to be replenished," he said.

items.title: There's a New Source of Inflation, and It's Put Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC Between a Rock and a Hard Place - The Motley Fool
items.summary: There's a New Source of Inflation, and It's Put Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC Between a Rock and a Hard Place  The Motley F
items.content:
Despite short-lived periods of volatility, it's shaping up as another phenomenal year for Wall Street and investors. With the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out as the primary catalyst, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.03% ) , S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.60% ) , and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +1.18% ) have catapulted to several record highs this year.
But expecting stocks to continue marching higher in the face of persistently elevated inflation is a tall order.
Kevin Warsh may be staring down a no-win scenario concerning inflation. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
In September, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised interest rates by 25 basis points, kicking off only the fourth rate-hiking cycle of the 21st century. While Trumpflation (Inflation specifically driven by President Donald Trump's policies) has frequently made headlines, a new source of inflation identified by FOMC policymakers has put the central bank between a rock and a hard place.
The Fed has identified a new source of inflation, and it can sink the stock market
The U.S. inflation rate has spent the last 67 months above the FOMC's long-term 2% target, prompting action by Fed Chair Warsh and his colleagues.
Two of President Trump's policies have been regularly singled out as core drivers of inflation : tariffs and the Iran war.
A newly published report ("How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices") by three New York Federal Reserve economists writing for Liberty Street Economics estimates that Trump's tariffs increased goods price inflation by 2.9 percentage points by February 2026.
New from the New York Fed: "By February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 pp to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly."
About one quarter of every point in higher tariff rates shows up in consumer prices within one year.
• A 10% across-the-board tariff yields a 2.6% rise in consumer goods prices after one year.
• About two thirds of the increase comes from pricier imports, which get passed through quickly.
• Another third comes from U.S. made goods, as producers face higher input costs and less import competition. This takes longer, about 6-12 months, to filter through.
Meanwhile, the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz, caused by the Iran war, represents the largest modern-day energy supply disruption. Gas and diesel prices have skyrocketed in its wake.
But combating Trumpflation is a relatively straightforward venture for the central bank. Attempting to deliver price stability amid a newly identified source of inflation is a different story altogether.
Shortly after Kevin Warsh became Fed chair, the FOMC meeting minutes singled out the AI infrastructure build-out as one of the core sources of elevated consumer prices.
On the one hand, overwhelming enterprise demand for graphics processing units (GPUs) , high-bandwidth memory (HBM), rack servers, and storage solutions has been a key growth driver for the U.S. economy and stock market. Ongoing supply shortages for GPUs and HBM, coupled with otherworldly demand, have afforded AI hardware companies exceptional pricing power.
The AI boom is transforming one of the biggest deflationary forces into a key source of US inflation:
Import prices for computer and electronic products surged +7.4% in the first 6 months of 2026, to 77.1 points, the highest since January 2016.
This also marks a +8.0% YoY jump, the largest annual increase on record.
This represents a historic reversal from a downtrend which persisted for over two decades.
Between 2006 and 2019, computer and electronic product import prices fell -30%, as improving technology and manufacturing efficiency consistently pushed costs lower.
Now, the AI investment boom is straining manufacturing capacity for semiconductors, servers, and electronic components, as companies race to build out AI infrastructure regardless of cost.
The AI revolution has flipped technology from a long-term source of deflation into a major driver of inflation.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) July 21, 2026
At the same time, this never-before-seen pricing power is adversely impacting consumers. The variables pushing up chip, memory, and storage prices are increasing the cost of laptops, smartphones, and other tech devices. This dynamic is unlikely to change unless the AI hardware supply shortage wanes and/or an AI bubble forms and subsequently bursts.
Inflation driven by the AI infrastructure build-out puts Fed Chair Warsh and the FOMC in quite the bind. If they leave interest rates unchanged for the foreseeable future, inflation may continue its upward trajectory, eventually harming the economy.
Conversely, if they get aggressive and raise rates multiple times over the next year, higher borrowing costs might halt the AI build-out in its tracks. Derailing a historically pricey stock market's No. 1 catalyst could knock the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals.
The unpleasant reality is there may not be a winning scenario for the Fed or Wall Street .

Oracle, in effort to reduce reliance on Nvidia, adds AI chips from Google, Cerebras, and SambaNova
Oracle ( ORCL ) is diversifying its AI cloud infrastructure, signing deals to bring chips from Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Cerebras ( CBRS ), and SambaNova ( SANS.PVT ) onto its networks as it looks to diversify beyond Nvidia's processors.
The move marks the first time Google is selling its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) for use within a third-party hyperscaler's data center rather than simply renting capacity to companies.
Cerebras's massive chips will provide AI inference capacity and AI agent processing power, while SambaNova's SN50 processor will handle agentic inference.
Oracle said its decision to bring on Google, Cerebras, and SambaNova's processors provides its customers with the right infrastructure for their particular needs.
Companies are increasingly working to reduce their dependence on Nvidia's AI chips to avoid being locked into a single supplier and to help contain costs.
Google, Amazon ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Meta ( META ), OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) either currently have or are developing their own custom AI chips. Like Google, Amazon is looking to offer its chips to third-party data center companies.
In June, Amazon's head of AI, Peter DeSantis, told Bloomberg that the company was in early discussions to begin selling its chips to outside data centers.
Nvidia has previously said it generates roughly half of its revenue from hyperscalers, making Google's move and Amazon's potential efforts of particular concern for the company.
But that doesn't mean Nvidia is in any immediate trouble. While the company's customers are clearly moving in on its home turf, they're still spending billions to buy up Nvidia's own chips.
Case in point: In addition to bringing on Google, Cerebras, and SambaNova's chips, Oracle said it is bringing Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 superclusters and Vera CPUs to its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).
In addition to Oracle's chip updates, the company said it's partnering with OpenAI on its Oracle AI Workspace. The platform allows users to access Oracle's tools via ChatGPT, letting them describe a task they want to accomplish and have the AI get to work.
The team-up also includes a new initiative called Oracle AI Security Mesh, which lets companies access OpenAI's cyber models to scan their software for flaws and vulnerabilities within OCI, fix them, and deploy them.
Correction: This is the first time Google is selling its chips for use in a third-party hyperscaler's data center. A prior version of this did not indicate that the chips have been sold to other data center operators.

Cloud infrastructure and corporate software firm Oracle Corp. (ORCL, Financials) is diversifying its AI chip supply strategy, lowering dependency on one source.
Oracle and Nvidia stated the cloud provider will grow installations of Nvidia's latest Vera Rubin systems to multi-gigawatt levels.
The firms did not reveal the amount of Oracle's arrangement, however Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously suggested Vera Rubin systems could earn up to $40 billion in revenue per gigawatt.
At the same time, Oracle is expanding its chip portfolio.
For the first time, the firm will provide Google tensor processing units, and it will also include inference processors from Cerebras and SambaNova, which is funded by Intel.
Even some of the Nvidia-based systems will employ Oracle's own networking technology, Acceleron, instead of networking processors from Nvidia.
And that important because AI workloads are increasingly demanding varied mixes of training, inference and network gear.
For Oracle, more options might make its cloud platform more attractive to clients, as well as increase its bargaining power with suppliers.
Up next is Oracle's investor day and management's aim to fund a fiscal 2027 capital-spending spree of about $90 billion to $95 billion.
