items.title: Ghanaian twin brothers and US woman plead guilty to $9m romance scam
items.summary: The group targeted elderly people across US and Europe, luring them into romantic relationship before persuading them to transfer large sums of money.
items.content:
By Gabriela Pomeroy Â  and Â  Thomas Naadi ,Â  BBC Africa ,Â  Reporting from Accra
Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.
The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.
The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.
Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (Â£6.7m).
While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.
As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.
Image source, US Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
Image caption, Jewellery was confiscated from the gang after they were arrested
Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement
Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster
Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman
In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.
Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.
In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (Â£5.9m).
He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.
The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

items.title: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
items.summary: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.
items.content:
Image caption, US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.
It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.
Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.
During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.
"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.
Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.
Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.
Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high .
The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.
The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.
US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.
Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.
Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".
Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told" , external , arguing that "nobody is getting fired".
US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.
Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.
That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.
Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.
"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.
"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."
Image caption, Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently
The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.
Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.
"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.
That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.
Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.
Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.
"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.
"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."
Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.
A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.
Image caption, Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households
The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.
Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.
The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.
Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.
The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.
Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.
If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

Gold Falls Below $4,000 as Investors Await Federal Reserve Rate Decision
Gold bars ©Adobe Stock Images Gold prices declined on Tuesday, briefly moving below $4,000 per ounce as investors assessed the outlook for U.S. interest rates ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy announcement on Wednesday and monitored diplomatic developments involving Iran.
At 05:58 ET (09:58 GMT), spot gold was trading 0.5% lower at $3,998.23 per ounce, while U.S. gold futures fell 0.6% to $4,013.17 per ounce.
The precious metal had gained 0.5% in the previous session before reversing direction, with market participants focusing on the possibility that the Federal Reserve will leave borrowing costs unchanged at its upcoming meeting.
Investors are awaiting Wednesday's Federal Reserve announcement following the central bank's decision in September to increase interest rates for the first time since 2023.
Market pricing indicates an approximately 10% probability of another rate increase at this week's meeting. However, elevated energy prices have maintained expectations that additional monetary tightening could take place before the end of the year.
Traders initially increased their expectations for an October rate increase after U.S. inflation figures exceeded forecasts.
Subsequent comments from Federal Reserve officials, which indicated that another increase in borrowing costs was not an immediate priority, moderated those expectations.
The upcoming decision will provide further information about the central bank's assessment of inflation and the potential direction of monetary policy.
Energy Prices Continue to Influence Inflation Expectations
Oil prices advanced during volatile trading on Tuesday, despite renewed diplomatic efforts aimed at preventing further escalation of the conflict involving the United States and Iran.
Persistently elevated energy prices remain a factor in inflation expectations, contributing to uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve's future interest-rate decisions.
Although diplomatic discussions have raised expectations of reduced regional tensions, the possibility of continued inflationary pressure from energy costs remains relevant to the monetary policy outlook.
A reduction in geopolitical tensions could help limit energy costs, while inflation remaining above expectations could sustain the possibility of additional interest-rate increases.
Market participants are also monitoring diplomatic initiatives intended to reduce tensions surrounding the U.S.-Iran conflict.
The latest negotiations have contributed to expectations that further military escalation could be avoided, although the outcome of the diplomatic efforts remains uncertain.
Developments affecting the conflict are relevant to energy markets, where oil prices have continued to fluctuate despite the renewed diplomatic activity.
Changes in energy costs could influence inflation expectations and, consequently, market assessments of future Federal Reserve policy decisions.
Gold's decline below $4,000 per ounce comes as investors evaluate the relationship between inflation, energy prices and U.S. monetary policy.
The Federal Reserve's September rate increase and subsequent inflation data have contributed to changing expectations for the timing of further adjustments to borrowing costs.
With markets assigning a relatively low probability to an immediate rate increase, attention remains on Wednesday's policy decision and any indications regarding the central bank's approach to inflation.
Gold traders are also following developments in the U.S.-Iran conflict and their potential implications for energy prices as the outlook for monetary policy continues to evolve.

"Until recently, European partners worked alongside us in our fields, and Chinese partners are still working there. Now, we're exploring the possibility of joint work with American partners," he said.

items.title: Warren Buffett sends timeless advice to S&P 500 stock investors - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Warren Buffett sends timeless advice to S&P 500 stock investors  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Warren Buffett sends timeless advice to S&P 500 stock investors
Warren Buffett built one of the largest fortunes in history by picking stocks. Yet the advice he has given ordinary investors for decades sounds almost boring next to his own record. It is advice that has outlived countless market fads. His instruction has stayed remarkably simple: buy a low-cost S&P 500 index fund and hold it.
That boring advice keeps giving. The S&P 500 set a fresh record high in early October, and Buffett's go-to recommendation continues to pay off for patient investors. The bigger story is how many people have taken his words to heart.
Buffett has made the same point in almost every format he uses. "My regular recommendation has been a low-cost S&P 500 index fund," he wrote in his 2016 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, published on Berkshire's website . He has also said he gave similar guidance to the trustee who will manage the money he leaves to his wife.
Also read: Warren Buffett has a stark message for stock market investors
The details of that plan are telling. In his 2013 letter, Buffett said the trustee should put 90% of the cash in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short-term government bonds, and he suggested Vanguard's fund. A man who could hire any manager in the world chose an index fund for his own family.
He repeated the message at Berkshire's 2020 annual meeting. "In my view, for most people, the best thing to do is owning the S&P 500 index fund," Buffett said. He added that nobody knows what the market will do tomorrow, next week or next year.
Timing, in his view, should not decide when people invest. In a 2017 CNBC interview, Buffett said the trick is to buy all the big companies through the S&P 500 and to do it consistently, according to The Motley Fool . He also urged investors to keep buying through thick and thin, especially through the thin times. Downturns, in other words, were buying opportunities rather than reasons to sell.
Related: Greg Abel's net worth: Buffett's successor's wealth as Berkshire's CEO
Buffett did more than talk about it. In 2007, he bet Protégé Partners $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a basket of hedge funds over 10 years, and he won. His Vanguard fund returned 7.1% a year, compared with an average of 2.2% for the hedge funds, as CNBC reported .
Fees help explain the gap. "Costs really matter in investments," Buffett has said. And index funds still keep those costs low while spreading money across many companies instead of one. A small fee difference can also add up to a large sum over decades of compounding.
The data keep backing him up. In the first half of 2026, 67% of actively managed large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500. Over the 15 years through June 30, 90.49% of them underperformed, and over 20 years the figure rose to 92.61%. Funds that were merged or closed count as underperformers in that tally.
The full-year picture was even worse. In 2025, 79% of active large-cap funds lagged the S&P 500, which tied the result to the low-cost index case Vanguard founder Jack Bogle made decades ago. In other words, the professionals Buffett warned about are still mostly losing to the benchmark.
Warren Buffett built one of the largest fortunes in history by picking stocks, especially those in one particular category.Bloomberg / Getty Images How his advice is shaping portfolios in today's market
Investors appear to be listening. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, part of the same Vanguard fund Buffett pointed his trustee toward, crossed $1 trillion in assets on June 3, becoming the first ETF ever to do so and overtaking State Street's SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust as the world's largest ETF, as reported by Reuters . Its parent mutual fund was the first index fund offered to retail investors.
Those who followed the advice have been rewarded. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has roughly quadrupled an investment over the past decade. That required no stock research at all, just patience. Reinvested dividends were part of that result, a reminder that staying invested matters.
Warren Buffett's $142 billion fortune hits a new milestone
Warren Buffett's farewell letter has 4 words for every investor
Warren Buffett shares a simple rule for surviving a market crash
The 3 biggest mistakes Warren Buffett made as Berkshire CEO
Part of the appeal is how little work it takes. Buying an S&P 500 index fund does not require investors to judge whether a business or its management team is outstanding, according to The Motley Fool . The outlet also noted that the S&P 500 and its predecessors have consistently delivered positive total returns over 20-year periods.
The irony is that Buffett's own company beat the market for decades. Berkshire posted a 19.7% annualized share-price gain from 1965 through 2025, compared with 10.5% for the S&P 500, yet Buffett still recommended index funds for family wealth, according to TheStreet . Few investors have the time, skill or temperament to repeat that record.
His plan was never meant as a one-size-fits-all formula. The 90/10 split he described was for his estate, and investors should build an emergency fund before putting money into an S&P 500 fund. An S&P 500 fund also holds no foreign companies, so some investors add an international fund alongside it.
What remains is the core idea. "If you bet on America and sustain that position for decades, you'd do far better than buying Treasury securities," Buffett said in 2020 . Markets will still have rough years along the way. For investors willing to stay patient and keep costs low, that bet is still paying off.

items.title: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war - BBC
items.summary: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war  BBC
items.content:
Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainer
US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum , an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

items.title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry
items.summary: President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% if a trade deal is not reached between the two countries.
items.content:
Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic
Honda executive Jennifer Thomas said a planned Jan. 1 increase to tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts would be “catastrophic” for the auto industry.
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% if a trade deal is not reached between the two countries.
Thomas urged the U.S., Canada and Mexico to preserve a trilateral North American trade framework rather than rely on bilateral deals.
An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025.
DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday.
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
"That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.
Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.
Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.
Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."
Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.
She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.
"Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."
Honda is the s econd-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor , but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.
While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.
"I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.
The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

World News in Brief: ‘No safe place in Ukraine’, IAEA calls for Iran nuclear inspections, Kenya hosts thousands of Ethiopians fleeing clashes
Peace and Security The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) on Tuesday urged continued international support for Ukraine’s population as Russian airstrikes intensify and humanitarian needs grow in advance of another bitterly cold winter.
The “relentless” attacks are targeting critical energy infrastructure, leaving millions without heat and electricity, and limited access to water and other essentials.
“The increase in long-range missile and drone strikes means there is no safe place in Ukraine,” said UNHCR director, Philippe Leclerc, adding that humanitarian operations have also come under attack.
Between September and mid-October, several security incidents affected agency personnel and partners, aid facilities or clearly marked vehicles involved in relief efforts.
UNHCR said displacement within Ukraine is expected to continue as evacuations from frontline areas increase, while nearly 5.2 million Ukrainian civilians continue to live across Europe as refugees.
UN nuclear watchdog still unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material
The UN’s nuclear watchdog still cannot confirm that none of Iran’s safeguarded nuclear material has been diverted, its chief told the Security Council on Tuesday – more than a year after Israeli and US military strikes cut off inspectors’ access.
“This can and must be rectified,” said IAEA Director Genera Rafael Grossi, adding that we know from our past work with Iran that constructive engagement is possible.”
Inspectors have not been able to return to the sites hit by Israeli airstrikes in June 2025 and joint Israeli and US attacks in early 2026.
The agency has seen no sign of work to repair or rebuild them, Mr. Grossi said, but satellite monitoring is no substitute for access on the ground.
The one exception is the Bushehr nuclear power plant, where inspectors are currently at work.
Iran’s atomic energy agency has cooperated in delivering the safeguards equipment needed to verify spent fuel there before it is moved to dry storage, expected early next year, Mr. Grossi said.
Rafael Grossi, head of IAEA, briefs the Security Council meeting on nuclear non-proliferation and Iran.
Normal inspections have not resumed, and Iran has not provided the information and access needed to verify previously declared nuclear material at its safeguarded facilities – both those hit in the attacks and those that were not – the IAEA chief said.
Of particular concern is Iran’s declared stock of 440kg of highly enriched uranium. The agency is also seeking access to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, which Iran declared just before the June 2025 strikes.
“Only diplomacy, underpinned by IAEA verification, can prevent nuclear proliferation in the long term,” Mr. Grossi said.
Kenyan authorities are at the fore of an emergency response plan to host more than 36,600 Ethiopian refugees who have fled escalating insecurity in the south, the UN Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ) said on Tuesday.
Recent fighting has triggered waves of displacement following a decades-long battle between forces from southern Ethiopia’s Somali and Oromia regions over boundary demarcations and resources.
Thousands of displaced Ethiopians are living with host communities.
UN agencies have joined the Government-led response – assessing needs and providing emergency supplies and technical support – including the World Food Programme ( WFP ) and UN migration agency, IOM , together with UNHCR.
On Tuesday, UNICEF in Kenya said therapeutic nutrition supplies had been delivered to a local hospital and the agency is supporting malnutrition screening, infant and young child feeding, safe water and hygiene services.
UNICEF has also provided four 10,000-litre water tanks and hygiene kits for about 1,000 households, alongside additional nutrition and sanitation technical support.

items.content:
AMD and Nvidia Split the AI Chip Market. 1 Stock Is Far Cheaper Today.
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) are two of the biggest names in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market. Their graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most popular options, and each is growing rapidly. However, from an investment standpoint, they are fundamentally different, especially when price tags are considered.
Nvidia is far cheaper than AMD, and this is something that investors can't ignore. I think that makes Nvidia the superior buy, but is there more to this picture? Let's take a look.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: The Motley Fool. Nvidia is defying the law of large numbers
Nvidia and AMD both make GPUs, which are general purpose computing units that can excel in just about any situation. This makes them the workhorse of the AI computing landscape, even as other custom AI alternatives grow more popular. Those custom chips are only meant to run one type of workload and will never fully replace GPUs.
In the early days of the AI arms race, Nvidia's products were far superior, which allowed it to capture an early lead. While AMD has improved its game, Nvidia's early lead has been tough to overcome. However, the law of large numbers suggests that the larger a company gets, the harder it is to grow. Therefore, if AMD is smaller, then it should be able to grow faster than Nvidia. If everything else is equal, a faster-growing stock will lead to better long-term returns, which would push AMD ahead of Nvidia as an investment option. The problem is, it isn't happening.
Nvidia is far larger than AMD. Nvidia's data center division (the sector most exposed to AI) saw revenue of $89 billion during the second quarter of its fiscal year (FY) 2027 (ended July 26). AMD's Q2 (which ended on June 30) saw revenue of $6.7 billion. The company's financial calendars are about one month apart, so this isn't a perfect comparison, but it's the best that investors can do. With AMD's data center division being more than 10 times smaller than Nvidia, it should have no problem growing faster, but Nvidia's growth in Q2 was 117% versus AMD's 107%.
While both companies are each delivering strong results, Nvidia is clearly growing faster despite its much larger size. But there's more to this analysis.
AMD and Nvidia also have non-data-center segments. However, Nvidia's other businesses are far smaller, and data center revenue accounts for the majority of Nvidia's $96.2 billion total. AMD's Q2 revenue was $11.5 billion, so other divisions make up a far higher percentage of its revenue. The problem is that these product lines aren't growing nearly as fast, so AMD's overall growth rate significantly lags Nvidia's.
AMD Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts. With this kind of growth disparity, you'd expect Nvidia to have a premium valuation relative to AMD, as it is growing far faster. But that's not the case.
Because these two are expected to grow rapidly over the next few quarters, I think valuing them based on forward earnings makes a lot of sense. From this perspective, AMD is basically three times more expensive than Nvidia.
AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts. That's a huge gap that doesn't seem logical, but that's how the market is pricing these two stocks. I think this is a huge mistake, and eventually it will correct itself so that these two stocks trade at roughly the same valuation. Whether that's caused by an AMD sell-off or an Nvidia rise is uncertain, but I'm confident that Nvidia will be the far better stock to own over the next few years. Its broad exposure to the AI arms race will boost the stock over the next few years, leading it to outperform AMD over the long term.

RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’
Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told
A group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.
One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.
Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.
Abdulkarim, of London, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service. He is accused of buying the vans used in the Fairford incident on the instruction of Ali.
Essghir, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, after initially being arrested at the scene near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September and then re-arrested on 20 October. He is accused of visiting RAF Fairford and filming around the facility on a video call with Ali before returning a month later in the convoy of vans.
Abdulkarim has been released on bail under conditions including the surrender of his passport, and Essghir has been remanded in custody. They will appear at the Old Bailey on 20 November.
Prosecutor Louise Gray alleged the defendants were in contact with an individual known as Ali who is now believed to be abroad.
She said that during the events of 27 September at the RAF Fairford base, five men who were arrested travelled in vans, parked and got out “and were told to do so by someone known as Mr Ali”.
One of them, she said, had claimed they were told there was a bomb in the van and called 999.
The court heard that the person calling stated that they were from London and that he was one of a group of five males. The caller told the police that they had been tasked to drive vans to the location for the purpose of a new business venture. When the vans arrived at the location, the organiser was in communication with them over the telephone.
Gray alleged he then told them to park the vans and to walk away from them. After they did that, the organiser told them to run as he had planted a bomb in the van. The caller indicated that he and his colleagues had run away from the vans and were now calling the police for help.
The defendants are believed to have known Ali for “a number of years”, she said.
Essghir is accused of travelling to RAF Fairford on 22 August and contacting Ali.
Abdulkarim is accused of buying mobile phones and collecting cash for Ali, as well as buying five vans including the three that were driven to RAF Fairford.
The court heard he had known Ali for 10 years and it was claimed the latter had been linked to a drone incident at the Israeli embassy.
Counter Terror Policing said they believed the foreign intelligence service involved in the case was Iranian.
The assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said: “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat.
“The public can help us with this, and as always I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”
A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national who was also arrested on 20 October on suspicion of aiding Iran’s intelligence service has been released without charge but remains on police bail after being arrested on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.
Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.
Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford. We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”

US Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Futures Ease As Traders Weigh Fed Path
The Morning Bull - US Market Morning Update Tuesday, Oct, 27 2026
US stocks look set for a slightly softer open, with the focus squarely on interest rate expectations rather than overnight equity moves abroad. Sentiment feels cautious as investors weigh solid US activity data against an approaching Fed decision.
The Chicago Fed National Activity Index printed at +0.07 for September, which points to modestly above trend growth. That reading supports the view of a still resilient US economy just one day before the Fed announces its latest interest rate decision.
A firmer growth backdrop can keep borrowing costs elevated, since policymakers have less pressure to cut aggressively when activity indicators run positive. Higher rate expectations tend to bite most in rate sensitive areas such as smaller caps and capital intensive businesses that rely heavily on refinancing.
The unresolved question is simple: Does a +0.07 activity print give the Fed enough confidence to signal a tighter path, or will officials lean on recent volatility in volatility gauges and global data to justify a more cautious tone on future hikes?
CoreWeave is in focus after expanding its AI cloud footprint with new computing capacity in Denmark and extending its Global AI Network into the Middle East and Asia Pacific. The firm is also in the spotlight as Anthropic's IPO filing draws attention to AI infrastructure providers and prior concern around CoreWeave's debt. Watch how customers respond to the larger network.
Visa faces a proposed collective £5 billion lawsuit in the UK over alleged anti competitive card payment fees. Law firms have asked the UK Competition Appeal Tribunal to allow an opt out action covering roughly 1,000,000 UK businesses. The key issue for investors is whether the tribunal approves the claim, which would set the stage for a long legal process.
Mastercard is caught in the same UK legal push, with the complaint targeting multilateral interchange fees over a six year period. The filing mirrors the case against Visa and seeks compensation for a wide pool of merchants. Attention now turns to how the tribunal frames any potential class, since that could influence eventual financial exposure and settlement talks.
Comfort Systems USA (FIX) jumped 7.18% after strong Q3 results, a record backlog, and analyst commentary that highlighted solid demand visibility.
Coherent (COHR) climbed 5.83% after StoneX initiated coverage with a Buy rating and highlighted indium phosphide capacity expansion.
Bloom Energy (BE) rose 5.49% following Q3 results that exceeded expectations, a higher 2026 revenue outlook, and a Barclays price target increase.
Nu Holdings (NU) fell 16.95% after Lula's surprise reelection in Brazil hit Brazilian financial stocks and the currency.
MercadoLibre (MELI) declined 7.81% as Lula's win in Brazil pressured Brazil-exposed U.S.-listed Latin American ecommerce shares.
DoorDash (DASH) dropped 6.10% after reports it is in advanced talks to acquire Instacart for about US$17 billion.
For US investors, the next stretch is defined by the Fed decision, a dense run of inflation and GDP releases, and a fresh wave of mega cap earnings led by Apple and Amazon.com.
Fed Interest Rate Decision Wed 28 Oct. The target rate previously sat at 4% and consensus also points to 4.0%. Any surprise move or sharper guidance on the path ahead could affect borrowing costs across mortgages, credit cards, and corporate debt.
Core PCE Price Index MoM Thu 29 Oct. Core PCE for September carries a consensus of 0.3%. A result above that mark could increase pressure on Fed officials to keep policy tight and could weigh on higher duration growth stocks.
GDP Growth Rate QoQ Adv Thu 29 Oct. Third quarter US GDP has a consensus of 3.2% after a previous 2.2%. A softer outcome could ease pressure on rates, while a stronger reading could reinforce the case for restrictive policy staying in place.
PCE Price Index YoY Thu 29 Oct. Annual PCE inflation previously printed at 3.4% with forecasts at 3.6%. A figure below that range could support the disinflation narrative and interest rate sensitive sectors such as housing and utilities.
Apple Mon 2 Nov. The Q4 2026 earnings release puts the spotlight on services and iPhone revenue. Any shift in guidance around those segments may help investors reassess expectations for cash generation and buyback capacity.
Amazon.com Thu 29 Oct. Q3 2026 results focus attention on retail margins and cloud profitability. The balance between online sales performance and AWS income may influence views on US ecommerce demand and big tech spending plans.
Energy and Oil and Gas have both gained over the past week, adding to strong 30 day and 1 year returns. Deals like EQT's plan to buy Range Resources and Ovintiv's Logan Energy purchase show large producers trying to scale around expected US gas demand and LNG exports.
If you own broad energy ETFs or US gas producers, the single data point to track is this Wednesday's EIA crude and product inventory report, because tighter US stockpiles can keep cash flows for the sector supported.
Real Estate : REIT deals contrast with rate pressure
Real Estate has firmed over the last 7 days and month while the 1 year number is close to flat. Private buyers are still active, with LXP Industrial Trust shareholders approving a sale and grocery anchored landlords like Brixmor and Phillips Edison expanding, even as higher borrowing costs hang over the group.
If you hold REITs, focus on Tuesday's US new home sales release, since slower sales would underline how current mortgage rates are affecting housing demand and developers' appetite to start new projects.
Tech & Semiconductors : AI buildout meets financing questions
Tech is slightly higher over the past week but softer over 30 days, while Semiconductors show a clear pullback on the month after strong year to date gains. Big AI infrastructure plans from Microsoft, Meta and others are generating orders for chipmakers and equipment suppliers, yet headlines about tighter funding for smaller AI data center operators are starting to matter for sentiment.
For portfolios with heavy chip or cloud exposure, Thursday's US Core PCE inflation reading is the key macro reference, since a firmer print can keep yields elevated and pressure sectors where investors rely most on long dated growth assumptions.
Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals & Biotech : Trial wins keep demand steady
Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals & Biotech have both risen over the past week and month on top of solid 1 year returns. Positive data on cancer and rare disease treatments from Merck, Pfizer, Mirum and others keep attention on new drug pipelines rather than day to day swings in discretionary spending.
If you use these sectors as a ballast in your portfolio, Thursday's US GDP and PCE inflation bundle is the main macro event, because a mix of steady growth and contained price pressures can support interest in earnings streams that feel less tied to the economic cycle.
Consumer Discretionary : Pressure under the surface of retail
Consumer Discretionary is down over the past week and year to date despite a slightly positive 30 day move. Earnings from Whirlpool and legal issues at retailers like Dollar General show how stretched budgets and price scrutiny can hit bigger ticket and lower income focused spending at the same time.
If you hold US retail or ecommerce stocks, Friday's US Employment Cost Index is worth watching, since slower wage growth would ease cost pressure for employers but could also temper how much consumers have to spend heading into the holiday season.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has confirmed the Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin was coordinated with Ukraine , saying it was “the right approach” to any engagement with Putin.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha‎ looks on prior to a meeting his Finnish counterpart Valtonen in Helsinki, Finland. Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPA Speaking alongside Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministers in Helsinki, Sybiha said:
“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process. This call was, as it was mentioned, coordinated with us, and this is the right approach. … I will say this once again, Ukraine wants to end this war. We have doable proposals and solutions. We are ready for partial ceasefires and a full end to hostilities. Of course, everything needs to be fair. We will not take any one-sided steps.”
Sybiha said that Ukraine was looking for “a new momentum” in peace talks with Russia, and to “define new role for Europe in our peace efforts.”
“So president Zelenskyy shared with his vision which signals our friends should convey directly to the Putin, and these signals were conveyed. Ceasefire … and another signal meeting with Putin. We are ready to meet with him. … Probably the only way to get …. new quality in our talks is a meeting at the level of president Zelenskyy and Putin.”
He later said that the negotiators can only discuss things up to a certain level, but key decisions can only be made by the heads of states.
He also added that Kyiv was “ready for the trilateral meeting” in the UAE next month, and “we will use every opportunity to bring peace closer.”
He also welcomed the limited ceasefire in Oleshky, saying it could “pave the way for other steps in the peace process as a confidence-building measure.”
But conceded that “the reality on the ground in Ukraine remains very tough” as a result of relentless Russian strikes.

Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a 90-minute phone call with Russia’s Vladimir Putin as they continue attempts to break the deadlock in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ( 10:41 ).
Finland’s Stubb welcomed the “frank and substantive” phone call, insisting that “ending the war requires direct discussions” with Russia.
Støre insisted “all our partners and allies were informed in advance” ( 13:43 ), despite scepticism or outright criticism from the Danish, Estonian, Polish and Swedish prime ministers ( 11:26 , 14:03 , 15:01 , 15:53 ).
But he conceded that “there remain significant differences in our respective positions.”
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for “real de-escalatory steps” in the conflict after his debrief with the two Nordic leaders ( 11:55 ).
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed the call was “coordinated” with Ukraine and said he hoped for “a new momentum” on peace talks with Russia ( 16:27 ).
But the Kremlin readout revealed that Russia’s Vladimir Putin blamed the EU and Nato for “confrontational policies” and demanded “full and unconditional recognition of the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation” ( 11:53 ).
The phone call took place just hours after a localised ceasefire kicked in the Ukrainian city of Oreshky after intense calls for humanitarian aid to be made available to the city’s residents ( 9:55 , 17:08 ).

Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, has warned that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is “testing us and testing Nato’s resolve” as he condemned hybrid threats and “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia ( 12:05 ).
Romania has summoned the Russian ambassador today, blaming Moscow for a recent fire at the state-owned Carfil defence plant in Brașov ( 16:10 ).
The Netherlands has dropped (again) from the 2027 Eurovision song contest amid “sensitivities” over Israel’s participation in the competition ( 12:35 ).

The US first lady, Melania Trump, has issued a brief statement confirming the humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine , which she was involved in organising.

In a statement, she said “timing was accelerated two days ahead of schedule to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid.”
She also added that “the ceasefire’s geographic area has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys. ”
Ukraine’s Sybiha has also pushed back against suggestions that it’s not a good moment for having a call with Putin.
“If you are at war, every decision, every step which support peace efforts is always timely. So that’s why we welcome such type of steps, efforts to speed up our negotiations.”
He also added that the European channel should not be seen as “the alternative” for the US-led talks, but “a supplementary track.”

Romania has summoned the Russian ambassador today, blaming Moscow for a fire at the state-owned Carfil defence plant in Brașov.
Fire at an industrial site next to a state-owned Romanian arms manufacturer in central Brasov County, Romania. Photograph: SRI/Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI)/AP The fire damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three people are being investigated for their involvement in the incident.
The Romanian security intelligence SRI confirmed yesterday that it had “identified a coordinated sabotage network from the Russian Federation” to be behind the arson attack, with “other attempts on targets in Romania. including international military facilities or those used for training the Ukrainian armed forces.”
Foreign minister Dan Neculăescu said in a post on X:
“MFA Romania summoned the Russian Ambassador today to convey a firm protest over the September 14th sabotage in Brașov. Evidence proves Russia’s responsibility for this unacceptable hybrid attack.
We also condemned Russia’s systematic strikes on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, a deliberate escalation violating international law and freedom of navigation, with global consequences.”
Earlier today, Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan , condemned the incident, calling it “a grave violation” of Romania’s sovereignty.
“ Let it be clear: these are not isolated, unrelated incidents; rather, they are part of a premeditated and coordinated campaign aimed at sowing division within our societies and undermining the commitment of European states to their own security and to collective defen ce.
We must not delude ourselves regarding the nature of this threat. This hybrid war has been ongoing for years, manifesting in various forms, all with the same objective: to weaken European states from within and erode the solidarity among them.”
Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, does not seem to be convinced by the idea of talking to Putin either.
The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsakhna, attends a panel discussion during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images In a post on X, he said:
“Only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously.
Every contact with Russia must convey Europe’s unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia , while making clear that Europe will not negotiate away the fundamental principles underpinning its security.
Ukraine wants peace, and Estonia supports all efforts to achieve it. But there is no indication that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations.
Russia’s goal is not merely to seize parts of Ukraine, but to subjugate the entire country and undermine Europe’s security order, founded on NATO and the EU.
A just and lasting peace requires increased pressure on Russia, tighter sanctions, action against sanctions evasion, Russia’s international isolation and unwavering support for Ukraine. We must show Russia through concrete action that, as long as its war continues, pressure will remain strong and Ukraine’s supporters will not abandon it.”
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has insisted that any peace “must be achieved on Ukraine’s terms,” joining a growing chorus of sceptical voices after an earlier call between Finland and Norway’s leaders and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Sweden's prime minister Ulf Kristersson attends the opening of the plenary session at the Finnish Parliament during the Nordic Council meeting in Helsinki, Finland. Photograph: Roni Rekomaa/Lehtikuva/Shutterstock Talking to reporters, Kristersson said that any peace settlement “must be brought about through strength, and not through appeasement towards Russia.”
“If talks lead to that, then talks are good. But my experience so far – based on the reports we received from German and French attempts at dialogue [with Moscow] – is that the results have been very, very modest.”
Kristersson added that given Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine , “I see nothing to suggest that they are seeking peace.”
“But we will surely receive an update on those discussions later today, and I am interested in that,” he said.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that attempts by ⁠the US and Russia to end the war in Ukraine “can never find solutions without Ukraine” ⁠and said any ⁠talks ​must also include European countries.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at an event in Singapore. Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty Images Merz was speaking at the Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore as ⁠he described diplomatic efforts to build a negotiating format with Moscow.
He said the end of ⁠the war depended “only on one person” and framed continued backing ​for Kyiv as a ‌defence of Europe’s political ‌order.
He said “as long as he [Putin] does not want ‌to end the war, we will support Ukraine” and that Europe was not just defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity but also “the entire political order of the European continent”.
Merz added that Russia , Ukraine, the United States and European countries ‌should be at the negotiating table and warned against a scenario where “Russia, perhaps China and the ​United States of America” end the war without Ukraine.
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk has also responded to Stubb and Støre’s engagement with Putin, giving a detailed account on the European consultations ahead of and after the call.
Poland's prime minister Donald Tusk attends a meeting in Hanoi. Photograph: Quang Nguyen/AFP/Getty Images Speaking before the cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said the call followed “consultations with me, among others, but primarily with president Zelenskyy and the US side … that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact given the planned ceasefire talks that may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
He said the UAE talks between Russia, Ukraine , and the US are provisionally planned for 4 November.
Tusk confirmed he had been briefed on plans for the call beforehand , with Norway’s Støre assuring him that he and Stubb were ready to take political responsibility for this rare engagement with Putin, and would stick to the agreed position of the coalition of the willing.
He said Finland’s Stubb then briefed him after the call, saying “both sides maintained their positions, ” and that “the European side’s impression during the call was one of very restrained optimism” about the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.
Tusk said he was “very cautions” about engaging with Russia and urged Stubb and Store to be “vigilant” in their talks with Putin, as “Russia’s agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement.”
He said Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of Nato’s northern and eastern flanks were “non-negotiable”.
Poland’s PM also stressed that despite the resumed dialogue, “nothing changes” in Europe’s “full support for Ukraine,” or collective views on “the [broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine.”
“ We should not have any illussions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing at, but I will remain in constant contact with all those who possess the good will and the belief that an agreement is possible – or at the very least, a ceasefire before winter.”
Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that “three, four nights ago,” “Russia lost 2,500 men” during one night. “This gives us an idea of ​​just how dire the further consequences of this war could be.”
Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre has offered a bit more colour on his and Stubb’s call with Russia’s Putin in a huddle with journalists in Helsinki just now.
Støre attends the opening of the plenary session at the Finnish parliament during the Nordic Council meeting in Helsinki, Finland. Photograph: Roni Rekomaa/Lehtikuva/Shutterstock He and Stubb had been initially given only 20 minutes to talk to Putin, but ended up speaking for 90 minutes, in a conversation he described as “substantive, focused on the issues at hand, and professional.”
“Much of what he said was already known – he [Putin] recalled his views on how the conflict evolved since 2014 – and we stated our positions. These are well-known views, which we were able to acknowledge and respond to,” he said.
The talks touched on what can be done to tackle most pressing issues, including attacks on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
But Støre conceded “there remain significant differences in our respective positions,” reiterating Norway’s continued support for Ukraine .
“We stand with Ukraine, defend its right to self-defence, and emphasise the need for a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” he said.
Støre also stressed that he and Finland’s Stubb spoke on behalf of their two countries only, “and no one else.”
Responding to criticism of their call from Denmark’s Frederiksen ( 11:26 ), he said that “all our partners and allies were informed in advance and received a detailed account afterwards.”
“If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view. I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well.”
Støre also stressed that the importance of the meeting in Abu Dhabi, first agreed as a result of the Oslo consultations that he and Stubb hosted.
In a brief section of the briefing in English, Støre again focused on pushing back against Frederiksen’s criticism:
“I believe that talking, having the right messages, is not wrong. Today these messages [are] coming out of the American administration; that is the only thing reaching Moscow. So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how it has to end.”
Russia is exploring the possibility ⁠of ⁠cooperation with ​partners from the ⁠United States in the resource-rich ⁠Arctic, president ​Vladimir ‌Putin ‌told a conference ‌of gas-exporting countries in Moscow.
Putin did not specify ‌whether the joint projects under consideration ​would involve extracting natural gas ⁠or other resources.
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are en route to the United States, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday, Moscow said, part of a deal that triggered a fierce Ukrainian and European backlash.
US president Donald Trump this month struck an agreement with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in exchange for Moscow releasing diesel onto global markets.
The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm legislative elections on 3 November and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies.
“At present, three tankers” with Russian fuel are on their way to the United States, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters on Tuesday. A fourth was expected to set off on Wednesday, he added.
The first US-bound tanker with Russian diesel departed last week. According to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler, it loaded nearly 300,000 barrels of diesel at the Primorsk terminal and was headed to New York.
In other news, the Netherlands has dropped (again) from the 2027 Eurovision song contest as public broadcaster NPO reversed its plans to pick up the baton after another broadcaster pulled out in August.
The 2020 competition took place in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Robin Utrecht/REX/Shutterstock The withdrawal is linked with “sensitivities” over Israel’s participation in the competition, NPO’s media director Jurre Bosman said, acknowledging the issue continues to “elicit various reactions in society and causes discussion and division.”
“Therefore, after consultation with the Board of Broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027,” he added.
This is the second time a Dutch broadcaster has dropped out of the competition: in August, the Avrotros, which usually selects the Dutch entry and broadcasts the show, had pulled out, paving the way for NPO to step in.
Ireland and Spain have also declared they will not take part in the 2027 competiton because of Israel’s involvement , and the Czech Republic pulled out over financial constraints. Iceland and Slovenia also didn’t take part.
The 2027 Eurovision song contest will take place in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas, after singer Darina Yotova, performing as Dara, won this year’s contest in Austria with “Bangaranga”.
